job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Aaron Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I wake early, pray, and have breakfast with my parents and my grandmother in our house in Westbury. Then I go to my father's hardware shop, where I keep the books and stock shelves for pocket money. I studied accounting with a good result and did six weeks at Mr Boateng's small tax practice, who is a friend from church. I send applications in the afternoons, and I go to evening prayer. My family has no money to spare for my loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's how I'd expect it, steady and sensible. I'd tell my father it's good news, because his shop and customers stay as they are. At church I'd say hard work and honest dealing will still count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's good for the world and still hard for me. There is no office job to be had around Westbury, and every month I fall further behind on the loan. I came out with a degree my family is proud of, and I have nothing to show for it yet except the shop's books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying to small local firms and ask Mr Boateng every month whether he needs help in tax season. I'd go door to door to the other small shops and offer to do their books at a fair price. I'd keep working for my father and not complain, because family helps family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy but patient. I try to trust that things work out, but I lie awake some nights doing sums. I don't tell my parents, because they have enough worries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you offer the other shops your bookkeeping rather than wait for a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a man should work with his hands where he can. Doing the books for two or three shops would earn something, and it would keep my skills sharp. My father says an idle week is a lost week, and I agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Boateng when you visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thank you for the six weeks, and ask honestly whether there is a place, even a small one. If not, I'd ask for his advice and a reference. He is a man who respects directness, and I'd rather ask than wait silently.

say: I'd tell my father it's **good news** for his shop.
At church I'd say **hard work** and honest dealing still count.
think: It's good for the world and still **hard for me**: no office jobs near Westbury.
Every month I fall further behind on the **loan**.
do: Apply to small **local firms** and ask Mr Boateng monthly about tax season.
Offer to do the **books** of nearby shops at a fair price.
Keep working for my **father** without complaint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a test, and people should hold on to what is solid. I'd tell my father to keep his customers' trust, because a machine can't hand over a bag of nails with a smile. At church I'd ask for prayer and community, because people will worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it frightens me. The work I trained for, checking figures and preparing returns, is the work software will do. Mr Boateng told me he's been offered a tool that does returns in minutes, and he doesn't know what to do. I don't use these tools. I feel I'm too slow for them, and I don't like how they make decisions I can't see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my uncle, who works in a bank, to teach me the basics once, and I'd go slowly. I'd stick with small firms and shops where people know me, because trust matters more there. I'd also look at an apprenticeship, since I believe in learning a trade beside someone older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, and a bit sad. I came up believing that study and hard work meet a job. Now I see the door narrowing and I can't tell my parents that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you trust apprenticeships more than a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a person watches you work and corrects you. In my father's shop he taught me by standing next to me, not with a book. If an accountant with thirty years would take me on and show me, I'd carry the man's bag.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to young people at your church who are starting degrees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say choose work where people need you in person, like teaching, nursing or running a shop, and keep faith that effort counts. I'd say do not borrow without thinking. I wish I'd been told that about my loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it is a great trial and the government must protect families first. I'd tell my father to keep his stock lean and not take on new debt. At church I'd ask us to look after each other, because some will lose their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my degree becomes paper. In two years there will be no firm hiring a young man to check numbers. I'd be twenty-five with a loan and nothing to my name. I feel it's unfair that it comes before anyone is ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work more hours at the shop, since a hardware shop will still sell nails and paint for a few years. I'd stop all spending that isn't food or the loan, and put the rest in savings. I'd also speak to the pastor about help for families and ask my parents if I could stay in the house as long as needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Afraid, and I won't lie about it. I feel like a man standing on a floor that is giving way. I'd pray more, and it would help a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Protect work for families who run small shops, and help young people with their loans. I don't believe in handouts as a way of life, but a loan frozen for people out of work would be fair. And make the big firms who replace people pay for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come around 2031. What does that mean for your father's shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It troubles me. A robot can lift and stack but it can't sit with a customer and judge what they need. For a time the shop stays, but I'd expect big chains to use robots first, and my father's margins to shrink. I'd talk to him honestly about that, once, and then follow his lead.

I'd ask the church to **look after each other**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is not nothing, and families should plan quietly. I'd tell my father to think about how the shop can serve people that big chains don't reach. At church I'd say we should teach the young ones a skill with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think five years gives me a chance to find a real place before the storm. If I'm taken on by a firm that values loyalty, I might be there two or three years, enough to hold a position. But if I wait, I miss the window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd press harder for a position, any position, with an honest firm, even if it is not in accounts. I'd learn the tools just enough that I'm not behind, starting with my uncle's help. I'd save in a plain account, not a gamble, and pay the loan as quickly as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little steadier. Five years means I can plan my marriage, someday, and not only my survival. But there's a knot there too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned marriage. How does that fit into this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a young woman at church, Abena, I think about, though nothing is settled. I wouldn't ask her family until I have steady work and the loan is under control. In the two-year version I'd put that off. In five years, I might hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd invest in things that take time, like the tools and a trade skill for the shop. In two years there's no time to build, only to hold on. With five, I can learn and still earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we should use it wisely. I'd tell my father he has time to hand the shop to the next generation properly. At church I'd say work, faith and family will carry us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years means I can build something. I'd be thirty-three, maybe married, with a small practice or a place in the shop. I'd still worry about being old-fashioned, but I'd have time to learn the new way and keep my values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd find a firm, learn from a senior accountant, and finish my professional exams. I'd learn the AI tools slowly, one task a year. And I'd grow my father's shop's books into a small service for other shops, so we'd both have something that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. It feels like a long field I can plant. I'd still pray, but with thanks more than with fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the shop to look like in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still in my family, with its name over the door. Maybe a second shop or a service for local builders. A hardware shop is a place where neighbours meet, and I'd like to keep that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope for from the young people coming after you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That they will learn a trade and a skill together, and not put their faith in a single path. If there's time, I'd teach young people how a ledger works by hand, because understanding is better than pressing a button.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because two years gives me no time to find a place, pay my loan or ask for a woman's hand. What would help is a loan freeze for those without work, an apprenticeship with a real accountant, and fair rules so firms don't simply drop young people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that a young man like me isn't asking to be carried. Give me a place where someone older will teach me, and I'll carry my share and more.

headlineQuote: Give me a place where someone older will teach me, and I'll carry my share and more.
portrait: Aaron, 23, has a **good accounting degree**, six weeks at a small tax practice, and lives with his parents and grandmother.
He keeps the books in his father's hardware shop and relies on church and **family** for support.
He avoids AI tools and trusts **learning from a person**, such as an apprenticeship.
His mood is anxious or alarmed in most worlds because jobs are few and the loan is heavy.
With ten years he feels **hopeful**, and hopes to build a small practice and keep the shop.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most: no time to find a place, pay the loan or plan a marriage.
whatWouldHelp: An **apprenticeship** with a real accountant, a loan freeze for people out of work, and fair rules for firms.
